entries.title: 5.0 magnitude earthquake strikes Egypt
entries.summary: The quake occurred at 3 a.m. local time about 22 miles north ⁠of the Egyptian city of Suez, the US Geological Survey said.
entries.content:
August 3, 2026

The quake occurred at 3 a.m. local time about 22 miles north ⁠of the Egyptian city of Suez, the US Geological Survey said.

A magnitude 5.0 earthquake struck off Egypt early on Monday, according to the United States Geological Survey.

The quake happened at 3 a.m. local time (0000 ​GMT) and hit an area about 22 miles (36 kilometers) northeast of the seaport city of Suez. 

The ​German Research Centre ‌for Geosciences (GFZ) measured the earthquake at magnitude 5.4 and ​recorded the depth of the quake at 6 miles (10 kilometers).

The Egyptian Red Crescent said it had activated ‌its emergency response plan in ‌the governorates where the earthquake was felt.

No immediate reports of damage or injuries

There were no immediate reports of casualties or property damage.

Humanitarian organizations urged residents to avoid buildings showing signs of structural damage.

Damaging earthquakes are uncommon in the northeast African country. The country's deadliest earthquake in modern history struck in October 1992, when a 5.8-magnitude quake shook the capital, Cairo, killing more than 500 people and displacing thousands.

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar

entries.title: Man arrested over death of British woman found in suitcase in Athens
entries.summary: The body of Scottish national Elisabeth-Jane Ross was discovered last month in a suitcase in a derelict building in Athens.
entries.content:
August 3, 2026

The body of Scottish national Elisabeth-Jane Ross was discovered last month in a suitcase in a derelict building in Athens.

A 26-year-old man has been arrested by Greek police in connection with the death of a British woman whose body was found in a suitcase in Athens last month.

"Officers of the Directorate for Combating Organized Crime have solved the homicide of a 38-year-old UK national, whose body was found inside a suitcase in an abandoned building in the Kypseli area on July 18," the Hellenic Police said on Sunday.

Police say suspect confessed

The victim, identified in British and Greek media reports as 38-year-old Elisabeth-Jane Ross from Scotland, arrived in Greece in late June and was last known to be in the Athens area on July 10. She was later reported missing.

Police said the suspect, a foreign national, confessed on Thursday and now faces charges including intentional homicide, robbery and firearms-related offenses.

"It emerged that the [suspect] placed the body in a suitcase and transported it to the abandoned premises. Furthermore, in the days that followed, the 26-year-old used the victim's bank cards to withdraw sums of money," police said.

According to reports, the suspect said the victim was already dead when he found her, although police made no mention of this in their statement.

A replica pistol and a knife were recovered from the suspect's home.

Greek police said international cooperation, including support from Interpol authorities in the US and UK law enforcement agencies, helped identify the victim despite advanced decomposition.

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar

entries.title: Pakistan: Suicide bomber kills 14 at anti-militancy protest
entries.summary: A suicide bomber has killed over a dozen people including police in an attack during a demonstration of citizens against militancy. More than 18 people were injured in the attack.
entries.content:
Pakistan

Pakistan: Suicide bomber kills 14 at anti-militancy protest

August 2, 2026

A suicide bomber has killed over a dozen people including police in an attack during a demonstration of citizens against militancy. More than 18 people were injured in the attack.

A suicide bomber killed 14 people and injured dozens more in an attack targeting anti-militancy demonstrators in the city of Kabal in Pakistan's northwestern Swat Valley.

Five police officers were among those killed at the event, which was staged outside a local police station to protest growing militant violence in the region and the state's inability to protect citizens.

Those gathered accused authorities of failing to act decisively against militants, saying residents want to live without fear after years of devastating violence.

The area was the home of Nobel laureate Malala Yousafzai, who was shot there by a Taliban gunman in 2012.

Hundreds of people were at the rally and social media video footage showed a speaker mid-sentence when an explosion rocked the area and sparked panic among demonstrators.

"The suicide bomber blew himself up when asked for a search in front of the police station," a local police official said.

No group has claimed responsibility for the crime.

A former Taliban stronghold

President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif both condemned the attack.

"Terrorists," said Zardari, "will never succeed in their nefarious efforts to harm peace, national unity and the writ of the state."

Pakistan has experienced a surge in militant attacks of late, with many targeting police and security forces.

The Swat Valley was a Taliban stronghold between 2007 and 2009, when Pakistan's military drove the Islamists out and re-established government control over the area.

The religious militants have recently resurfaced, however, with the Pakistani Taliban, known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, being particularly active.

The TTP is separate from, but allied with, Afghanistan's Taliban rulers and has been a source of tension between the neighboring countries.

Pakistan says the TTP and other militant groups are carrying out attacks in the country with the support of Afghanistan's Taliban rulers and has promised to continue targeting the TTP and its support network.

Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez

entries.title: Ukraine hits targets deep inside Russia, killing eight
entries.summary: Ukrainian drone strikes inside Russia killed eight people overnight in attacks that targeted military and civilian infrastructure. Russia said Moscow's forces downed 635 drones in the assault.
entries.content:
Europe

Ukraine hits targets deep inside Russia, killing eight

August 2, 2026

Ukrainian drone strikes inside Russia killed eight people overnight in attacks that targeted military and civilian infrastructure. Russia said Moscow's forces downed 635 drones in the assault.

Ukrainian drones rained down on numerous military, energy and civilian infrastructure sites deep inside Russia on Sunday, killing at least eight people overnight.

Russia's Defense Ministry said its forces downed 635 drones over the course of the attacks.

Two people were killed in the city of Engels on the Volga River when drones hit residential buildings. Another apartment complex in nearby Saratov City was also damaged.

Three people were reported killed and two injured in the Udmurtia region (1,300 kilometers from Ukraine), and another three killed and five injured in Belgorod according to local officials.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday said Kyiv had targeted an oil refinery in Saratov and a military base that is home to Russian long-range bombers in Engels.

Zelenskyy said the attacks were his country's answer to Russian aggression and thanked Ukrainian forces for taking the war "back to where it came from."

Kyiv said fires had damaged both sites and that its forces had also struck an oil depot in the western Kaluga region.

Unverified video uploaded to social media sites purported to show fires burning at the Saratov oil facility.

Why is Ukraine targeting Wildberries warehouses?

Ukraine again targeted the online retailer Wildberries in its attacks, striking a logistics warehouse in Samara — more than 800 kilometers (500 miles) from Ukraine's front-line positions.

Sunday's attacks on Wildberries were just the latest onslaught on the retail giant, which Kyiv says aids Russia's military.

Kyiv has attacked nearly a dozen Wildberries warehouses since July 18.

No casualties were reported at the facility and local management said that a fire at the site had been brought under control.

Although the number of drones that Russia claims to have downed cannot be confirmed, the figure is indicative of the scale of Kyiv's effort to strike Russia deep inside its own territory as it defends itself against an army that launched a full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022.

The Wildberries attacks are seen as an attempt to bring President Vladimir Putin's war home to Russia's citizens, applying pressure to the country's already anaemic economy in hopes of finally ending Moscow's ongoing invasion.

Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez

entries.title: Ceuta: Most who breached border have left, Spain says
entries.summary: Nearly all of the more than 50,000 migrants who breached the border this week have returned to Morocco, according to Spanish officials. At least 72 people died in the border rush. DW has more.
entries.content:
Published July 31, 2026last updated August 3, 2026

Nearly all of the more than 50,000 migrants who breached the border this week have returned to Morocco, according to Spanish officials. At least 72 people died in the border rush. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Ceuta returning to normal but work remains, local official says
  • Madrid says 72 people died in the border rush
  • Right-wing leaders call for migrant expulsions, security reinforcement
  • Italy's one-month suspension of the free-movement Schengen deal takes effect
  • Spain's PM Sanchez calls for an urgent teleconference of EU interior ministers
  • DW correspondent says thousands of migrants still in Ceuta
  • Germany's Merz calls on Morocco to take back the irregular migrants 'without delay' 

We've closed the blog. Read here for updates on the situation in Ceuta, Spain's North African territory on the weekend of August 1-2.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Thank you for reading

Thank you for reading

Most of the 60,000 migrants who crossed into Spain's North African exclave of Ceuta had walked back to Morocco by Sunday, but some stayed on in the hills surrounding the city.

Spanish authorities continued searching for bodies in the waters near the stretch of urban beach that tens of thousands of migrants had breached days earlier.

We'll have more on the news about what exactly happened and why this many people decided to swim to Ceuta in the coming days.

Skip next section Morocco blames social media misinformation, people smugglers for border chaos

Morocco blames social media misinformation, people smugglers for border chaos

Morocco's Interior Ministry said on Sunday that the recent border surge in Ceuta was fueled by misinformation on social media, human trafficking networks and a Spain court ruling banning the immediate return of migrants arriving by sea.

The statement was the first from the Moroccan government since the mass border breach on Thursday and Friday, during which Spain says between 50,000 and 60,000 migrants entered Ceuta.

Morocco said around 40,000 people were involved in the mass crossing at Ceuta, while 1,135 were stopped while trying to enter Melilla, Spain's other North African exclave.

The ministry also said 11 people had died. Ten of them died by drowning while attempting to cross the border, the ministry said, with one person dying after falling from a rocky area.

The ministry added that Moroccan officials were checking reports from their Spanish counterparts that 72 people died.

Skip next section Far-right politicians call for migrant expulsions, security reinforcement

Far-right politicians call for migrant expulsions, security reinforcement

The border crisis in Ceuta has sparked debates in Spain and across Europe about the Spanish government's migration policy.

Many governments in Europe have sought to curb immigration, but Spain has pursued a different approach, recently announcing a plan to provide legal status to up to 500,000 undocumented migrants.

Pedro Sanchez and his Socialist government have been heavily criticized this week by politicians from Spain's right and far-right parties.

The leader of the opposition, the conservative People's Party's Alberto Nunez Feijoo, has traveled to the exclave, where he slammed Sanchez for failing to prevent the border rush.

The leader of the far-right Vox party, Santiago Abascal, who was also in Ceuta on Sunday, blamed the Socialist government for the migrant surge, which he described as "an invasion."

He said the surge was an "act of war" and an "attack on the sovereignty and security of Spaniards."

Abascal also said Sanchez was "a danger" to the country, and called for the EU-Morocco agreement, which functions as a partial free trade area, to be scrapped.

Far-right influencer and Member of the European Parliament Alvise Perez called for migrants to be expelled during a confrontation with a crowd of rival protesters in Ceuta. Much of the city's population is of Moroccan descent.

Perez had to shelter in a bar before being escorted away by police.

Sanchez and his government have also been criticized by other right-wing politicians in Europe, most notably Italy's Interior Minister Antonio Tajani.

Italy has suspended free movement with Spain, even though both are part of the Schengen Area.

Skip next section Most migrants return but Ceuta still on edge as death toll climbs to 72

Most migrants return but Ceuta still on edge as death toll climbs to 72

Relative calm had returned to Ceuta on Sunday, but the city remained on edge following the deadly border rush.

Local officials have warned that the city's recovery has just begun, while right-wing politicians are blaming the Socialist government in Madrid for chaotic scenes that unfolded this week in the Spanish North African exclave.

Spanish Civil Guard ships were searching the waters around the city on Sunday for more bodies after between 50,000 and 60,000 migrants breached the border with Morocco.

Nearly all of them had walked back to the Moroccan side of the border by Sunday, according to officials in Ceuta, normally home to around 84,000 people.

At least 72 people died during the crush on Thursday and Friday, the Spanish government representative in Ceuta, Miguel Angel Perez, said.

Some drowned, while others were killed in a stampede at a breakwater barrier and a border fence.

Perez added that medical services have treated more than 1,000 people.

He said while the situation in the exclave had improved significantly, work remained to be done for the city to return to normal.

On Saturday, authorities installed a 500-meter (1,600-foot) floating barrier in the waters off Ceuta to boost border security, as well as reinforcing police and army patrols.

Skip next section WATCH: Spain installs floating barrier to stop Ceuta sea crossings

WATCH: Spain installs floating barrier to stop Ceuta sea crossings

Skip next section What to know if you're joining us on August 2

What to know if you're joining us on August 2

  • Spain said on Saturday migrant crossings into its North African territory of Ceuta had stopped overnight after authorities began installing a 500-meter floating barrier at the border with Morocco.
  • More than 50,000 people crossed into Ceuta by land and sea on Thursday in an unprecedented surge, Spain said more than 48,000 were returned to Morocco within 48 hours.
  • The death toll from the mass crossing rose to at least 67, with migrants dying from drowning or being crushed while attempting to scale border barriers.
  • European Union interior ministers will meet for emergency talks on Tuesday, with 22 member states, including Germany, calling for coordinated border measures.

  • Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez criticised Italy's decision to suspend Schengen travel with Spain for one month.

  • Spain has reinforced police and military deployments in Ceuta. Authorities stressed that migrants entering the territory irregularly cannot travel onward to mainland Spain or elsewhere in the Schengen area.

Skip next section Emergency meeting of European interior ministers to take place Tuesday

Emergency meeting of European interior ministers to take place Tuesday

An emergency video meeting of European Union interior ministers is to be held on Tuesday, according to Ireland's prime minister, Micheal Martin.

"As Presidency holders, Ireland will convene a meeting on Tuesday of the EU Justice and Home Affairs Council... to discuss developments in Ceuta," the Irish leader wrote on Saturday.

The Republic of Ireland currently holds the EU's rotating presidency and Irish Justice, ​Home ⁠Affairs and Migration Minister ⁠Jim O'Callaghan has been tapped by Martin to lead the call. 

Skip next section EU's von der Leyen says lessons must be learned to improve resilience

EU's von der Leyen says lessons must be learned to improve resilience

In a social media post on X, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she had "offered support to Spain from the first moment" and that most of those who stormed the Spanish North African territory of Ceuta this week had been returned to Morocco.

"Not a single person reached mainland Spain or the rest of Europe," she said.

The head of the EU's executive said, however, that the bloc's "strong system" of border protections "needs to be further strengthened."

While emphasizing coordination, she said lessons must be learned "to improve our European resilience."

 

Calling for vigilance and coordination, von der Leyen ended her statement by saying, "Fighting illegal migration requires solidarity and a united European response."

Skip next section France says no need for Spain to leave Schengen

France says no need for Spain to leave Schengen

French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez on Saturday was cited by news agency AFP as saying that despite France's own increased security along its shared border with Spain, "We are not asking for Spain's suspension from Schengen."

Addressing calls by European politicians for Spain to be temporarily booted from the freedom of travel agreement, Nunez said: "Spain does not need to leave the Schengen zone. It's absolutely not on the table. We have great cooperation with Spain."

Italy announced a one-month suspension of visa-free movement with Spain on Friday after tens of thousands of migrants stormed the Spanish exclave of Ceuta, overwhelming authorities.

Spain has assured EU partners that irregular entry into Ceuta does not confer a right to remain in Spain, travel to the mainland, or move freely throughout Europe.

Skip next section DW reporter: Ceuta locals feel 'a mix of of fear and anger'

DW reporter: Ceuta locals feel 'a mix of of fear and anger'

DW correspondent Jan-Philipp Scholz reported high tensions in Ceuta on Saturday morning, despite the claims by the Spanish authorities that the situation in the exclave was back under control.

"I've still seen clashes between police, military and migrants, also between locals and some migrants this morning," he said.

While the overwhelming majority of irregular migrants has already left the area, Scholz pointed out that thousands were still in Ceuta and Spanish authorities were growing "increasingly robust" in their efforts to get the rest to leave. Most migrants did not receive any food or water, and all the shops in the area are closed, Scholz pointed out.

"They are pushing the people away from the beaches or from overwhelmed reception centers that cannot take any more people in," he said.

He also said that locals were feeling "a mix of fear and anger" in the wake of the incursion.

"Most people did not want to come out of their houses yesterday. And most people are still staying inside today."

Skip next section WATCH: Could the Ceuta crisis help Trump in the midterms?

WATCH: Could the Ceuta crisis help Trump in the midterms?

Donald Trump has called the migrant crossings into Spain an "invasion." US political analyst Michael Yaki unpacks the political strategy behind the rhetoric.

Skip next section IN PICTURES: Some migrants tell DW they don't want to go back to Morocco

IN PICTURES: Some migrants tell DW they don't want to go back to Morocco

Skip next section Spanish police start installing floating barrier

Spanish police start installing floating barrier

In Ceuta, Spanish authorities started laying a new pneumatic barrier on the sea border with Morocco.

The 500-meter (1,640-feet) long barrier is designed to stand 30 to 70 centimeters (12-28 ​inches) above the water line and up to one meter (3.3 feet) below it. It will run parallel to a line of anchored buoys, forming a channel that would be patrolled by Spanish law enforcement.

Many of the migrants that entered the Spanish territory of Ceuta in recent days achieved that by simply swimming around the existing barrier with Morocco and gaining access to the Spanish-controlled beach.

Spain's El Mundo daily published a video online of a Guardia Civil boat installing the barrier.

Skip next section Most EU nations join call for emergency talks after Ceuta crisis

Most EU nations join call for emergency talks after Ceuta crisis

In an open letter, 22 out of the EU's 27 members demanded a video meeting of the bloc's interior ministers on Saturday.

The meeting should be convened "as a matter of urgency" to coordinate a joint response to the situation in Ceuta, and "prevent further uncontrolled crossings."

Earlier on Saturday, Spain's Pedro Sanchez also called for a meeting of interior ministers.

Skip next section Sanchez: Spain managed to 'fully restore control of the border'

Sanchez: Spain managed to 'fully restore control of the border'

In less than 48 hours following the border incursion in Ceuta, the Spanish government has managed to "fully restore control of the border, provide extensive humanitarian aid, repatriate virtually all migrants who crossed irregularly, and prevent any unauthorized movement toward continental Europe," according to Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez.

"This has been achieved in close coordination with Moroccan authorities and with very little support from other European states," he added in the letter addressed to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and other top EU officials.

He also pointedly noted that Spain was "one of the European Union's least porous external borders, with a number of irregular entries that is half of that recorded in Italy in recent years (2021–2026), for example."

The Spanish leader also expressed confidence that a meeting of EU interior ministers would help "establish a common response to situations of this kind and reaffirm that the security of our external borders is a responsibility shared by all member states, and not just by those on the Union's front lines."

entries.title: Greece: Fire brigade helicopters collide as wildfires spread
entries.summary: The crew of one of the helicopters is reported to be safe but the search for the second is ongoing. Prime Minister Mitsotakis has warned of "extremely difficult" days ahead, while one expert has referred to a "megafire."
entries.content:
August 2, 2026

The crew of one of the helicopters is reported to be safe but the search for the second is ongoing. Prime Minister Mitsotakis has warned of "extremely difficult" days ahead, while one expert has referred to a "megafire."

Two fire brigade helicopters collided mid-air in Greece on Sunday, as firefighters continued to battle fierce wildfires around the Gulf of Corinth.

The fire service said the two aircraft collided in the Psatha area, just to the west of the capital, Athens, adding that search and rescue teams were "immediately mobilized to locate and assist the crews."

Television footage showed one of the helicopters explode and plunge to the ground in flames after an apparent rotor collision.

Greek public broadcaster ERT reported that the crew of one of the helicopters had been found and were safe. The fate of the crew of the second helicopter initially remained unclear.

Greece wildfires: 'Extremely difficult' days ahead, says PM

The accident came as Greek firefighters continued to battle wildfires on multiple fronts. Three firefighters died in recent days in the line of duty, two in Crete and one in the Peloponnese.

The fires are being exacerbated and spread by winds of up to 100 kilometers (60 miles) per hour, with Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis warning of "extremely difficult" days ahead.

"When the winds blow with such force, even the dozens of aircraft we have at our disposal cannot operate safely," he wrote on social media.

"There are moments when nature and the intensity of weather phenomena surpass any human planning and any operational capability."

Just to the north of Psatha in the neighboring town of Porto Germeno, nearly 500 firefighters were attempting to keep a blaze from approaching the western outskirts of Athens after it scaled a mountain overnight.

Footage released by Greek police showed officers going door to door on motorcycles in the nearby hilltop village of Agios Nektarios, sounding sirens and shouting "Is anyone there?" as they urged residents to evacuate.

On Friday, firefighters evacuated 254 people by sea – often the last escape route for isolated coastal communities – followed by another 12 on Saturday.

"We could not believe what we were seeing," Nikos Georgopoulos from the laboratory of forest management at the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, told state TV channel ERT. "The fire spread extremely rapidly."

Greece: man arrested on suspicion of arson

Further west and on the opposite side of the Gulf of Corinth, some 100 firefighters were fighting another blaze in Aigialia in the northern Peloponnese region.

Meanwhile, a 44-year-old man was arrested on Sunday on suspicion of deliberately starting a new fire which broke out late Saturday on the popular Ionian Sea island of Cephalonia.

The National Observatory's climate tracker meteo.gr said early estimates indicated that over 6,500 hectares (16,000 acres) had been burned in separate fires around the Gulf of Corinth.

Meteorologist Theodore Giannaros said that the fires around Porto Germeno are "likely, if not almost certain … [to] be classified as a megafire."

Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez

entries.title: Small insects, big damage: The global ant trade is booming
entries.summary: Legal or not, the trade in African ants bound for Europe is booming. What do hobbyists find appealing about these insects, and what risks does the trade pose to ecosystems, including power outages?
entries.content:
August 2, 2026

Legal or not, the trade in African ants bound for Europe is booming. What do hobbyists find appealing about these insects, and what risks does the trade pose to ecosystems, including power outages?

They are unusual pieces of evidence that regularly appear in Kenyan courtrooms: thousands of ants packed into tiny containers.

Since 2025, such finds have been presented in court several times. Staff from the Kenya Wildlife Service discovered them during baggage inspections. In multiple cases, they identified thousands of specimens of the sought-after Messor Cephalotes species also known as the Giant African Harvester Ant. A single queen can fetch more than €200 ($230) on the market.

The export of wild animals is generally prohibited in Kenya. Due to high levels of poaching — particularly involving elephants and rhinoceroses — many African countries have introduced tough laws against wildlife trafficking.

Kenya has also tightened its legislation. Under these rules, a Chinese national who attempted to export ants was sentenced last April to one year in prison for biopiracy. Given the growing scale of smuggling and its ecological consequences, the judge said the sentence should serve as a deterrent.

It was already the second major ant-smuggling case in 12 months. The previous year, the wildlife service stopped four men who referred to themselves as the "Ant Gang." Among them were two 19-year-old Belgians who were trying to smuggle 5,500 queens to Europe. They were fined around €5,000 each.

Whenever such cases arise, authorities often call entomologist Dino Martins to the airport. "I was shocked," he said. "Not only by the sheer number of ants, but also because they were queen ants."

The seized insects were young queens that had been dug up from nests in the ground, according to Martins, who has led several research institutes in Kenya and is regarded as one of Africa's leading ant experts, These queens have wings that allow them to fly away and establish new colonies.

"When you collect queens at this critical moment, you interrupt a key stage in the creation of new colonies," he said, adding that Kenya's ecosystems are also affected because ants transport grass seeds, helping to regenerate the savannah.

A new niche hobby

In Europe, keeping ants as pets has become increasingly popular, particularly among young people. Colonies are housed in glass terrariums where a queen produces offspring and establishes an entirely new population.

One person who keeps ants as a hobby is Michael Meier, who asked not to be identified by his real name. While at university, he wanted a pet that required little attention.

"With ants, it doesn't really matter whether I feed them today or tomorrow," he said.

At one point, Meier kept almost 30 colonies in a room specially set up for them. Today, he has four. He admits that exotic species are considered especially attractive to ant enthusiasts because they do not hibernate.

"That way, you can enjoy the animals all year round," he said.

On the websites of numerous online shops, ants can be ordered through the mail with just a few clicks. "African ants" is a category commonly used to attract customers. Among the species on sale is the very one repeatedly discovered at Kenyan airports.

Anyone who asks dealers how the ants reach Europe receives few answers. Even sellers who advertise "import permits" have declined to answer media inquiries. The trade operates in a legal gray area.

Under the international wildlife trade agreement monitored by the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), ants are not considered a threatened species. Their trade is therefore neither prohibited nor regulated globally.

Kenya, meanwhile, bans the export of all wildlife. But unlike ivory, ants can easily be smuggled out of the country in hand luggage or through the mail.

High profits, low risk

The online trade in wildlife has expanded rapidly beyond the ant business, says Russell Gray. Working with an international team, he investigated the issue for the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime.

"The key finding is that this is no longer a marginal problem hidden away on obscure websites," Gray said. "Today, we see it happening on popular platforms such as Facebook."

Last year, Gray's team examined more than 60 online platforms. They found 266,000 advertisements that included prices. The combined value of wildlife listings amounted to around $66 million. Insects were not even included.

"If we looked at the entire online wildlife trade," Gray concludes, "we would probably be talking about a market worth billions."

Chris Shepherd, a biologist at the US-based Center for Biological Diversity, which advocates globally for biodiversity conservation, is deeply concerned.

The Kenyan cases demonstrate that compared with other forms of crime, such as drug trafficking, profits are high while "the risks are significantly lower," he said. Once rare species begin commanding high prices, organized criminal networks become interested in the trade.

Shepherd therefore calls for stricter regulation. In open letters, he has urged CITES to address the ant trade. He is particularly concerned about the consequences for ecosystems.

Ants have no lobby

Those consequences are already making headlines in Germany.

Entire colonies of North African large gland ants regularly cause power and internet outages in southern Germany by nesting inside electrical distribution boxes.

To address the issue, local government representatives from Austria, Switzerland and southern Germany met at an ant conference in the summer of 2025 to exchange experiences.

Climate change, bringing higher temperatures and less frost, has made conditions in Central Europe increasingly suitable for the species.

Shepherd notes that most ants probably arrive in Europe through plant imports rather than the online pet trade. Even so, he argues that the hobby market poses risks as well. No one can guarantee that colonies will never be released into the wild.

Ant keepers such as Meier are familiar with these debates, which frequently take place in online forums. Meier advises owners who lose interest to either pass colonies on to other enthusiasts or euthanize them properly rather than releasing them.

For Shepherd, that is not enough. As long as the international ant trade remains largely unregulated, he says, it will continue to pose a risk.

Translated from German by Silja Fröhlich

entries.title: Germany news: DB hampered by 'organized irresponsibility'

entries.content:
Germany

Published August 1, 2026last updated August 3, 2026

DB chief Evelyn Palla wants to overcome the culture of ''organized irresponsibility" by empowering new decision-makers within the railway operator. Bavarian brass musicians have wrapped up a 72-hour concert. DW has more.

  • DB's Evelyn Palla sets 2035 as goal for completing major reforms within railway company
  • Pride events are taking place in several German cities a week after a deadly attack on a Pride march in Berlin

Skip next section We're closing the blog

We're closing the blog

Thanks for reading the weekend edition of the Germany blog. We'll be back with the latest headlines on the morning of August 3.

Skip next section Audience boos AI-generate stage design at Richard Wagner festival

Audience boos AI-generate stage design at Richard Wagner festival

The audience at the annual Richard Wagner festival in Bayreuth booed after a performance of "Götterdämmerung" that was staged on a set that was designed with the help of artificial intelligence (AI).

The staging featured a collage of images which appeared to confuse members of the audience, who booed when curator Marcus Lobbes and his team took the stage at the end of the performance on Saturday evening.

The audience, however, warmly applauded the singers and musicians, as well as conductor Christian Thielemann.

Ahead of the performance, organizers had said AI would be used on stage for the first time as "an image-generating force."

The singers of Wagner's epic drama would be "the fixed point within a visually seething cosmos of light, texture, history, and association, amidst projections that erupt, constantly shift, and merge into one another," the festival's organizers said.

The AI-generated projections were drawn from images that Lobbes and his team had pre-selected, which included scenes from previous performances of Wagner's "Ring" cycle of four music dramas and from historical themes.

The collage, which included a commemorative stamp marking German reunification, images of former chancellor Helmut Kohl and the World Trade Center towers after the September 11 terror attacks, appeared to confuse the audience, according to German news agency dpa.

Skip next section Chancellor Merz 'very stable and strong' – Söder

Chancellor Merz 'very stable and strong' – Söder

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is in a "very, very stable and strong" position, according to Bavarian Premier Markus Söder, who said on Sunday that he is "totally convinced" that Merz will "remain chancellor."

Söder, of the Christian Social Union (CSU), the conservative Bavarian sister party of Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU), made the comments in an interview with public broadcaster ZDF amid falling poll ratings for the chancellor.

With some party members fearing a poor performance in upcoming state elections in autumn, speculation has grown that Merz could be replaced as head of the government.

Söder dismissed such suggestions and warned that such a scenario could lead to demands for an early federal election "which would only promote one thing: extremists gaining power."

Instead, Söder urged party members and supporters to "concentrate on the work which needs to be done" and called for "togetherness" and "unity."

Skip next section Rhine water levels at record low

Rhine water levels at record low

Water levels in the Rhine river reached historic lows in Cologne, Düsseldorf, Bonn, Duisburg and other cities this weekend due to continuing high temperatures and a lack of rain.

In Cologne, the Rhine fell to just 67 centimeters (26 inches), two centimeters lower than the previous record set in 2018. By Sunday, the water level (or Pegel in German) had risen back up to 69 centimeters.

In Düsseldorf, however, the water level dropped to just 21 centimeters on Sunday, also two centimeters lower than the previous low point.

Low water levels are driving up transport costs for the business sector and placing a particular burden on industries that rely on the transport of bulk goods. Inland vessels are forced to carry significantly less cargo or suspend operations entirely.

In addition to freight shipping, the exceptionally low water levels on the Rhine are also causing difficulties for tourism and passenger shipping.

According to one company, the Köln-Düsseldorfer Deutsche Rheinschiffahrt GmbH, numerous trips have had to be canceled, and certain vessels have been unable to dock at specific piers along the Rhine due to the receding waters.

"Freight traffic on the Rhine is already reacting to the falling water levels," warned Thilo Schaefer from the German Economy Institute (IW), telling the Rheinische Post newspaper that the reduced loads on river barges force transport costs upwards and also puts motorways and railways under more pressure.

Christoph Ploss, a conservative (CDU) politician who acts as the German government's maritime coordinator, warned that "low water levels must not become a ball and chain for the German economy."

Skip next section Bavaria: drunk man falls asleep on autobahn

Bavaria: drunk man falls asleep on autobahn

A 41-year-old man was found drunk and asleep next to a German motorway in the early hours of Sunday.

Police said they received several calls from drivers who had spotted the inebriated pedestrian stumbling around on the A96 Autobahn near Memmingen in the southern state of Bavaria.

When officers arrived on the scene, they found the man asleep under a crash barrier.

The man, who was said be "absolutely dunk" was taken to a cell to sober up.

Skip next section Brass musicians wrap up a 72-hour performance in Bavaria

Brass musicians wrap up a 72-hour performance in Bavaria

Around 1,850 brass musicians finished an unprecedented, 72-hour live performance with a church service In St. Jacob's church in Nürnberg, Bavaria on Sunday.

The event involved over 140 bands from across the German state, with them swapping roughly every 90 minutes to ensure there are no interruptions longer than 10 seconds.

The record is now to be confirmed by Germany's Record Institute.

Bavaria's Premier Markus Söder agreed to act as patron for the event.

In a statement, he conservative politician praised the "enthusiasm" and "passion" displayed by the musicians, and said that music creates "a strong sense of community — not only inside the circle of brass musicians, but also between them and their listeners."

Skip next section Kölln cereal recalled due to 'foreign objects'

Kölln cereal recalled due to 'foreign objects'

German cereal producer Kölln is expanding its contamination warning for its cereals with chocolate over fear that "foreign objects" might have gotten into the packages.

"We would like to emphasize that, to date, there has been only one known case in which a hard plastic part from our production process was found in a package. The foreign object was not baked into the product," they said in a statement online.

The warning now applies to cereal packages of 375 grams with batch numbers L6165, L6164 and L6235. The packages are also marked with "best before" dates of 17.04.2027, 16.04.2027 and 05.06.2027.

Kölln urged customers to return their product to supermarkets, promising a full refund regardless of having a receipt.

Skip next section Deutsche Bahn chief Evelyn Palla blasts 'organized irresponsibility' in the company

Deutsche Bahn chief Evelyn Palla blasts 'organized irresponsibility' in the company

The culture inside Germany's Deutsche Bahn (DB) is already shifting but the current crisis will take years to overcome, the head of the national railway company told Germany's Welt am Sonntag.

CEO Evelyn Palla criticized the old decision-making process in DB, saying that the central management often made big decisions on the operative level.

"The people in the headquarters, who made those decisions, don't have any responsibility for implementing them in the field," Palla said. "They have to be implemented by colleagues who are out there. But they say 'I didn't make this call, and it also doesn't work for me.' Then the headquarters says 'I have no operational responsibility, those people in the field did not implement [the decision] properly.' In the end it was something like organized irresponsibility."

She told the paper that much has been "reformed" and "slimmed down" since she took the reins of the state-owned firm last October, and that multiple administration levels inside DB had been cut.

"But all of that does not make for a better (Deutsche) Bahn," she added. "Things will only change when the management changes, when decentralized units take responsibility and live with it."

In the interview published on Sunday, she also said that the German railway network was "run into the ground by 25 years of saving money" and that tangible improvements will take time.

She pointed to DB's 200-year anniversary coming in 2035, saying that "this should be the year when the worst is behind us."

Skip next section We are resuming our coverage

We are resuming our coverage

Welcome back to our coverage of top news stories from Germany on this early August weekend.

On Sunday, Berlin is preparing for an anti-Islamist march in response to the deadly terror attack which shook Germany to the core a week ago.

In Bavaria, over1,800 brass musicians are hoping to break the record for the world's longest concert as they near the end of the unprecedented 72-hour live performance.

And Evelyn Palla, the head of Germany Deutsche Bahn, is decrying "organized irresponsibility" inside the troubled railway company.

We will be bringing you more on these and other stories from Germany in this live blog.

Skip next section We've paused coverage

We've paused coverage

Thank you for reading the weekend edition of our blog about Germany and be sure to check in on Sunday morning to stay up to date with the latest headlines out of the country.

Skip next section WATCH — Hamburg Pride draws 300,000 after Berlin terror attack

WATCH — Hamburg Pride draws 300,000 after Berlin terror attack

Hamburg's Pride parade went ahead under heightened security, one week after a 21-year-old drove a van into crowds at Berlin Pride. The attack killed one person and injured 29 others.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: Germany widens deportations to Afghanistan

IN DEPTH: Germany widens deportations to Afghanistan

Earlier this week, Germany for the first time deported a man with no criminal record to Kabul. 

This set a precedent that sparked vociferous protests: 260 people heeded the call of an anti-racism alliance and came to demonstrate inside the airport's departure hall, accompanied by a police escort.

Read more about Germany's policy on deportations to Afghanistan.

Skip next section Klingbeil urges for solidarity with Spain over Ceuta border breach

Klingbeil urges for solidarity with Spain over Ceuta border breach

German Vice Chancellor and Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil on Saturday called on Europeans to stand by Spain amid the debate over the surge of migrants into Ceuta.

Footage showing tens of thousands of migrants crossing into Spain's North African exclave of Ceuta raised concerns across the European Union.

"Migrants were used in an attempt to divide Europe," Klingbeil said.

He noted that Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez had restored control quickly and that most migrants who entered Ceuta had already returned to Morocco.

"Especially in situations like these, Europe must not allow itself to be divided," Klingbeil said.

Klingbeil's comments come after Italy officially suspended the Schengen agreement with Spain for one month in response to the mass crossing in Ceuta.

Skip next section Popular German national park closed after storm leaves 1 dead

Popular German national park closed after storm leaves 1 dead

A popular park in eastern Germany was closed to visitors on Saturday after a storm caused damage and left one person dead overnight.

A 38-year-old man was killed on Friday evening near the Felsenbühne open-air theater in Rathen when he was struck by a falling tree.

Ten other people were injured, three of them seriously, while 40 people were evacuated.

Emergency crews resumed clean-up operations on Saturday.

Authorities closed the area between the Bastei rock formation, the villages of Rathen and Hohnstein, and the Polenztal valley, citing ongoing safety risks for visitors.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: Germany weighs the future of minijobs

IN DEPTH: Germany weighs the future of minijobs

When Anahita Abdollahi starts her shift, she first checks her emails to make sure she's up to date on all the library requests.

The 26-year-old master's student from Iran describes her job as a "part-time librarian" — she helps people find books they need for their studies, answers phone calls, and waters the plants.

This type of employment is known in Germany as a "minijob," a system that allows millions of workers, including students, to avoid paying income tax or social security contributions.

entries.title: Moscow restaurant blast a 'brutal terror attack,' mayor says
entries.summary: The deadly explosion outside an upscale Moscow restaurant at Kudrinskaya Square was a "brutal terror attack," Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said, promising the perpetrators would be punished. But many questions remain.
entries.content:
August 2, 2026

The deadly explosion outside an upscale Moscow restaurant at Kudrinskaya Square was a "brutal terror attack," Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said, promising the perpetrators would be punished. But many questions remain.

An explosion at a restaurant in central Moscow killed at least three people, including the suspected bomber on Saturday night, authorities said.

Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin described it as a "brutal terrorist attack."

"Law enforcement agencies are investigating the circumstances of the incident. Those responsible for this crime will certainly be found and face the punishment they deserve," he said in an online post on Sunday.

Russia's Anti-Terrorism Committee said a woman carrying  "a homemade explosive device" tried to enter the restaurant on Kudrinskaya Square but was stopped by a security guard.

The device exploded at the entrance, killing the woman, the guard and a restaurant patron.

What do we know about the explosion?

State news agency RIA Novosti reported that at least 21 other people were injured in the blast, which occurred shortly before 8 p.m. local time (5 p.m. UTC).

The restaurant's website said the venue had been closed on Saturday for a private event.

Heavily armed law enforcement officers sealed off the area and launched an investigation.

Authorities did not immediately identify those they believed to be behind the attack.

Russia has faced several attacks since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022. They blamed a ‌series of assassinations and attempted killings on Kyiv. Russian officials have yet to comment on any possible Ukrainian involvement into the Kudrinskaya Square blast.

Ukraine hits targets deep inside Russia overnight

However, Ukraine used drones to attack other parts of Russia on Saturday evening and early on Sunday, including a bombing which targeted an apartment block and killed two in the city Engels, some 900 kilometers (560 miles) southeast of Moscow.

Russia's Defense Ministry also said Kyiv struck a warehouse belonging to Wildberries, a major online retailer in Russia, with the Ukrainian drones hitting a site in the Samara Oblast, deep inside Russian territory. Regional Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said it was not immediately clear if there were any casualties.

Russian officials also reported over a 100 Ukrainian strikes in the Belgorod Oblast, which borders Ukraine. They said Kyiv forces used artillery, rocket launchers, and drones, leaving 14 people injured.

Over 200 Ukrainian drones have allegedly been shot down during the wave of attacks.

Overall, Russia claimed 635 downed Ukrainian drones overnight.

Meanwhile, at least one person was killed and seven wounded in the Russian attack on Ukraine's Kherson, with the attack involving artillery fire.

In Dnipro, seven passengers were wounded in a drone strike on a minibus, with the regional military administrator Oleksandr Hanzha describing it as a "deliberate and cynical attack on civilians."

At least nine people were killed and 33 injured in Russian strikes on Kyiv earlier this weekend.

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar and Rana Taha

entries.title: Indonesia: At least 5 dead in ferry fire
entries.summary: Search and rescue officials report some 41 missing after a fire on a ferry near the Indonesia island of Madura. The cause of the blaze remains unclear.
entries.content:
Indonesia

Indonesia: At least 5 dead in ferry fire

August 2, 2026

Search and rescue officials report some 41 missing after a fire on a ferry near the Indonesia island of Madura. The cause of the blaze remains unclear.

At least five people have died and another 41 are missing after a ferry caught fire in Indonesia on Sunday morning, authorities have confirmed.

The Mutiara Sentosa 2 ferrywas carrying a total of 271 passengers and crew members from Indonesia's second-largest city, Surabaya in East Java, across the Java Sea to Makassar in South Sulawesi.

Search and rescue officials said 225 people had been rescued by Sunday afternoon but that an operation was still ongoing.

Some passengers reportedly jumped overboard and were picked up by a nearby ship. Four other vessels were on standby nearby but could not approach because of the risk posed by flammable material on the ferry, officials said.

What have Indonesian authorities said?

"Based on preliminary reports from the field, passengers are waiting to be evacuated by the vessels in the vicinity of the incident site," said Muhammad Masyhud, a senior official at the Indonesian Ministry of Transportation.

"The safety of passengers and crew is our top priority. We are continuously coordinating with all relevant parties to ensure that the evacuation process can proceed quickly, safely, and effectively," he added.

The fire, the cause of which remains unclear, was reported by the ship's captain who, according to officials, has not been in contact since.

Are shipping accidents common in Indonesia?

Indonesia is an archipelago of more than 17,000 islands where marine accidents are a regular occurrence, due to a combination of unpredictable weather conditions and lax safety standards.

Last month, a ferry transporting more than 70 people sank while sailing near Selayar, a small tropical island south of the much larger Sulawesi.

At least four people were found dead, and 14 others remained missing until the end of the search operation.

Edited by: Rana Taha
